title: Introduction to Data Science
text:
Collaborative Notes
The Fall 2026 collaborative notes supplement the instructor-authored Introduction to Data Science book. They give students practice explaining data-science concepts and working through a Git and GitHub review process.
The notes are maintained in the ids-f26 repository. Students contribute through topic branches and pull requests. The repository contains two kinds of presentation. A topic presentation explains a method or idea and belongs under topic/; a final-project presentation reports an original project and belongs under final/.
Each topic presentation needs a short catalog entry in its relevant topical chapter. Final-project presentations are collected in the Final Project Presentations chapter. In both cases, the slide deck is the substantive contribution; contributors do not need to rewrite slides as prose.
The topical chapters and final-project chapter organize and link to presentations; they do not duplicate the instructor book.

section: Clone and Render the Notes Locally
text:
Clone and Render the Notes Locally
Keep a local copy of these notes so that you can render presentations before opening a pull request. Place the ids-book and ids-f26 repositories in the same parent folder. If you plan to contribute, fork statds/ids-f26 on GitHub first, then clone your fork. Replace GitHub_Username below with your GitHub username:
cd path-to-your-course-work
git clone https://github.com/GitHub_Username/ids-f26.git
cd ids-f26
git remote add upstream https://github.com/statds/ids-f26.git
git remote -v
git status
If you only want a local copy for reading and rendering, clone the shared repository directly instead:
git clone https://github.com/statds/ids-f26.git
cd ids-f26
Use the course Python environment that you already chose while working through the instructor book. Do not create another virtual environment or install packages inside ids-f26. From the ids-f26 repository, set ENVIRONMENT_DIRECTORY to that environment’s path and activate it:
ENVIRONMENT_DIRECTORY=/path/to/your/environment

# macOS or Linux
source "$ENVIRONMENT_DIRECTORY/bin/activate"

# Windows with Git Bash
source "$ENVIRONMENT_DIRECTORY/Scripts/activate"
Confirm that the selected interpreter is the course environment before rendering:
python --version
which python
make check-tools
Render the notes and all accepted presentations with:
make render
Quarto writes the local site to _book/index.html. Open that file in a browser and inspect the page or slides before requesting review. While developing one presentation, render only that source file:
make render-one FILE=topic/last-name-topic/index.qmd
The _book/ directory is generated output and must stay out of commits. If a render fails because a package is missing, first verify the active interpreter and ask the instructor before adding a dependency to the shared course environment.

text:
Topic Presentations
The private course syllabus contains the assessment policies for topic presentations. This public chapter documents the presentation order, topic options, schedule, and contribution workflow without reproducing grading details.

Presentation Order
The topic presentation order will be finalized in class. Each student will contribute one digit to the random seed. The current seed produces a provisional order; after the contributed digits replace it, the same seed will reproduce the final order on every render.
#| eval: true
#| echo: true
import csv

with open("roster.txt", newline="") as file:
    roster = csv.DictReader(file, delimiter="\t")
    presenters = [
        f"{row['Last Name']}, {row['First Name']}"
        for row in roster
    ]

import random

## seed jointly set by the class, with one digit from each student
random.seed(0)  # replace 0 with the sum of the contributed digits
random.sample(presenters, len(presenters))
The displayed order is provisional until the class sets the seed. The final order will establish priority for topic selection and the default sequence for topic presentations. Some topics have prerequisites, so the instructor may adjust the schedule. Students may exchange slots by mutual agreement. Record an approved change through a pull request and notify the instructor.


Selecting a Topic and Task Board
Discuss your proposed topic with the instructor at least one week before the presentation. Topics may have prerequisites; for example, decision trees should ordinarily precede random forests and gradient boosting. text:
Assignment Workflow
Graded work is submitted through the designated Classroom 50 repository, not through the instructor book or collaborative-notes repository.
Each assignment submission must use one .qmd source file that solves all assigned problems. Label every problem clearly inside that file so that the source and rendered PDF are easy to navigate. Use the homework template as the starting point for the required structure.
Follow the detailed Git workflow in Project Management, especially Exercise 2.7. That workflow explains how to inspect a repository, create a branch, stage named files, review diffs, write meaningful commits, inspect history, and preserve evidence of the work.
Fall 2026 assignment requirements are:

Accept the assignment through the course site and clone the resulting Classroom 50 repository.
Develop the single .qmd source file on a descriptive branch, solving all assigned problems and labeling them clearly.
Make at least ten small, meaningful commits for every assignment. Do not create empty commits or split meaningless changes merely to reach ten. Each commit should record a real development step and use an informative, imperative message.
Preserve the complete branch history. Record the branch name, commit hashes and messages, and concise command results in the assignment source or wherever the assignment specifies.
Push the branch and render the assignment before submitting the PDF through the designated course workflow.

The ten-commit requirement applies to each assignment repository, not to the semester notes repository as a whole. Graded assignments remain private in Classroom 50 and are not submitted as public pull requests unless an assignment specifically says otherwise.
Keep generated files out of the repository unless the assignment explicitly requests them. Use Git from the command line rather than GitHub’s file-upload interface, and never commit credentials or large data files.

Syllabus Check
Use the syllabus and its linked resources to answer the following questions. The questions are intended to clarify course expectations rather than reward memorization; consult the relevant source when uncertain.

Where should you look for private course materials, permanent instructor notes, and Fall 2026 student presentations?
What percentage of the grade comes from style, participation, homework, topic presentations, the midterm project, and the final project? How does the final-project requirement differ between STAT 3255 and STAT 5255?
How are the 20 topic-presentation points divided among approval and preview, the oral presentation, and the pull request? When is each component due?
What must a topic-presentation pull request contain?
When are the final two instructional weeks, and what attendance and participation are required during them?
What are the proposal, instructor-meeting, presentation, and final-report deadlines for the final project?
How does the maximum available homework credit change during the 48 hours after a deadline? What happens after 48 hours?
What kinds of AI use are encouraged? Which graded components must be completed independently, and when must AI use be disclosed?
According to the linked email-etiquette guide, what greeting, subject line, closing, and identifying information should a professional email contain?
What should you check before emailing a question whose answer may already appear in the syllabus, assignment instructions, or course notes?
How long should you ordinarily allow for an email response, and which conversations are better handled during office hours?
According to PEP 8, how many spaces should each indentation level use, what line lengths are recommended, and where should imports appear?
What skills can you practice with Git Exercises, and why are small, meaningful commits preferable to one large final commit?
What is the difference between collaboration and copying when completing homework or a project?
Using the UConn Library resources on avoiding plagiarism and citing sources, what material must be quoted, paraphrased, cited, or otherwise attributed?
Under UConn’s academic-integrity policy, why are students expected to ask before using an outside resource when an assignment does not explicitly authorize it?
Read UConn’s Student Code and its academic-integrity appendix. What responsibilities do students have for their own work, proper attribution, and avoiding an unfair advantage?
Why are command-line operation, Git, reproducible code, and Quarto treated as data-science skills rather than merely software preferences?
What information and demonstrated qualities would help the instructor write a useful recommendation letter?
